title: Servo Pulse Width Explorer
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Robotics and Computational Thinking
description: Move a servo arm from 0 to 180 degrees and see how the angle sets a 1 to 2 ms pulse inside a 20 ms PWM period and a duty_u16 value from about 3276 to 6553.

educational.topic: Servo motor control with PWM pulse width
learningObjectives: Explain how a servo angle from 0 to 180 degrees maps to a pulse width from 1 ms to 2 ms.
Explain why the 20 ms period stays the same while the pulse width changes.
Convert a servo angle to a duty_u16 value with int(min_duty + (angle / 180) * (max_duty - min_duty)).
prerequisites: PWM duty cycle, frequency, and 16-bit duty values (Chapter 7)

controls.label: Sweep / Stop sweep
controls.purpose: Sweep 0 to 180 to 0 degrees in 5 degree steps every 20 ms, like the Servo Sweep Code.

controls.label: Reset calibration
controls.purpose: Restore min duty 3276 and max duty 6553.

assumptions: The servo reads a 50 Hz PWM signal.
The servo angle is linear in pulse width between the calibration points.
limitations: The arm eases toward the target angle; real servo speed depends on the motor and load.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Multiple linked representations with concrete numeric readouts
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Direct manipulation of the angle with synchronized arm, readout, gauge, and timeline; optional sweep demonstration
keyQuestions: Which part of the PWM signal tells the servo its angle?
Why does the period stay at 20 ms for every angle?
Why might two servos need different min and max duty values?
commonMisconceptions: A bigger duty cycle makes a servo spin faster, like a DC motor.
The servo angle is set by the PWM frequency.
Every servo reaches exactly 0 and 180 degrees at 3276 and 6553.
assessmentOpportunities: Record pulse width and duty for 0, 45, 90, 135, and 180 degrees.
Find the duty at 45 degrees (4095) and at 180 degrees with max duty 7000.
Explain in writing how the robot points the servo straight up.
